readings.title: A handover between two shifts
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A small warehouse changed shifts at midday. The next team sometimes moved boxes before learning that one aisle was being repaired. The main obstacle was repair information missing from handovers. A spoken reminder could be forgotten when one shift ended early. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a review of recent handover notes. Supervisors compared written records with the times when staff first entered each aisle. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated a single shared log improved awareness. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a brief written safety handover at every shift change. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: important information must survive a change of staff. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in a handover between two shifts, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Reporting a near miss
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
In a catering kitchen, a worker caught a loose floor mat before anyone fell. Colleagues were unsure whether to report an incident without injury. The main obstacle was uncertainty about reporting small hazards. The lack of harm made the risk seem unimportant even though the mat remained in use. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used anonymous examples from staff meetings. The manager invited workers to describe hazards and checked the existing reporting guidance. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated early reports exposed correctable risks. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a simple near-miss form and prompt mat replacement. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: prevention starts before an injury. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in reporting a near miss, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Instructions beside a machine
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A workshop displayed operating instructions in a folder. New employees could not consult them easily while wearing protective equipment. The main obstacle was guidance placed away from the task. Workers had to leave the machine and remove gloves to turn pages. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used observation of a supervised training session. A qualified trainer noted each moment when workers paused to remember a step. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated a short visible checklist reduced hesitation. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced approved step cards mounted at safe viewing points. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: safety instructions should be available at the moment of use. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in instructions beside a machine, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Making a delivery briefing clear
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Drivers received a daily route update by message. Several people missed a change to the unloading entrance because it appeared at the end. The main obstacle was critical information buried in routine text. The message began with general news and used the same formatting for every detail. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a comparison of two briefing formats. Managers asked drivers to identify the change after reading each version once. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated a short action line was noticed more often. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced briefings that lead with the required safety action. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: message order can affect safe behaviour. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in making a delivery briefing clear, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
A useful plan for workplace safety and communication must take account of the people who will use it. An idea may look complete on paper and still create difficulties during an ordinary week. Organizers therefore tried the workplace communication programme on a small scale and invited comments from users with different schedules. They recorded benefits as well as the time and resources needed to provide them. Some findings supported the original aim, while others suggested that the method should change. The group published both kinds of result instead of presenting the trial as a simple success or failure. This allowed residents to discuss the next step with a clearer understanding of its possible effects.

translation.referenceAnswer: 关于职场安全与沟通的有用方案必须考虑实际使用它的人。一个想法在纸上看似完整，平常使用时却仍可能出现困难。因此，组织者小规模试行该服务，并邀请时间安排不同的使用者提出意见。他们既记录益处，也记录提供这些益处所需的时间和资源。有些发现支持最初目标，另一些则表明方法应当调整。团队同时公布两类结果，而没有把试行简单说成成功或失败。这让居民能更清楚地了解可能的影响，再讨论下一步。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the workplace safety team about a community activity related to workplace safety and communication. Explain how different people can participate, what should be recorded, and how the results should be shared.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the workplace communication programme. People have noticed repair information missing from handovers, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
